title: Makaton, PECS and objects of reference
blurb: Recognise how Makaton, PECS and objects of reference work, who each one suits, and how to use them correctly on the ward.
question: Callum, 21, has a severe learning disability and visual impairment. He does not use pictures or signs, but his support worker hands him a cup before every drink and a towel before every bath. On admission, how should the nurse continue this approach?

teach.h: Three tools, three kinds of user
teach.body: Makaton, the Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS) and objects of reference are augmentative and alternative communication tools. Each suits a different person. Makaton adds signs and symbols to speech. PECS teaches a person to start a request by handing over a picture. Objects of reference use real objects that stand for an activity, person or place. In plain English: find out which tool the person already uses and use it the same way they do.
teach.cite: The Makaton Charity; Pyramid Educational Consultants (PECS); NHS learning disability SLT services

teach.h: Makaton: signs and symbols with speech
teach.body: Makaton is a communication programme that uses symbols (pictures), signs (gestures) and speech. Signs are used WITH speech, in spoken word order, to give extra clues. Signs help people with no speech or unclear speech; printed symbols help people with limited speech and those who cannot or prefer not to sign. It has a Core Vocabulary taught first and a larger topic-based Resource Vocabulary. Some people use it for life.

teach.caption: PECS was developed in 1985 at the Delaware Autism Program by Andy Bondy and Lori Frost.

teach.h: PECS: the person starts the exchange
teach.body: In PECS the person hands a picture to a communication partner and receives the item or activity shown. The key idea is initiation: the person learns to approach someone and start communication, rather than waiting to be asked. Later phases build sentence strips ('I want' + picture), answering questions and commenting. On the ward, keep the person's book within reach and respond promptly when they hand you a picture.

An object of reference is an object that stands for an activity, person or place, in the same way that a word does: a cup for a drink, a towel for a bath, a seat belt buckle for a car journey. They suit people who find speech, signs, photos and symbols hard, including many people with profound and multiple learning disabilities or sensory impairment. Used consistently, they help a person anticipate what is next, understand when something is finished and make choices.
teach.cite: NHS learning disability speech and language therapy resources (HPFT; LPT)

teach.caption: Tools can be combined in one person's total communication plan.

teach.h: A starting point, not a rule
teach.caption: The speech and language therapist and the person's own history decide the plan; on the ward, continue what they already use.

teach.h: Using a person's tool on the ward
Scenario: Callum on the surgical ward
teach.body: Callum, 21, has a severe learning disability and a visual impairment. His support worker brings his object bag. Before each drink the nurse places his own cup in his hands; before washing, his towel. She uses the same objects in the same way, gives him time to feel them and waits for his response before starting. She records the objects and their meanings in his care plan so that the night staff do the same.

teach.text: Common mix-ups: Makaton signs are used alongside speech, not instead of it; PECS is about the person starting an exchange, not staff showing picture cards to give instructions; and an object of reference only works if the same object is used for the same activity every time.

items: Makaton: signs + symbols + speech; signs in spoken word order; Core and Resource Vocabularies.
PECS: six phases, from physically assisted exchange to commenting; the person initiates.
Objects of reference: a real object stands for an activity, person or place.
Use the person's own tool, in the same way, every shift; record it.
Tools can be combined within total communication.

summary: You can now explain how Makaton, PECS and objects of reference work and match each to the people it suits. You can continue a person's own communication system consistently on the ward and avoid the classic errors in using each one.

A.q: A healthcare assistant asks how Makaton is meant to be used. Which description is correct?
options: Signs replace speech so the person is not confused by words
Signs are used with speech, in spoken word order
Signs follow British Sign Language grammar and word order
Symbols are used and signs are kept for people who are deaf
A.why: The Makaton Charity states that signs are used with speech, in spoken word order, to provide extra clues about what someone is saying.

whyNot.0: Makaton supports speech; it does not replace it.
whyNot.2: Makaton signs follow spoken word order, not BSL grammar.
whyNot.3: Makaton signs are used with people who have no speech or unclear speech, not kept for deaf people.

A.q: What is the main skill taught in the early phases of PECS?
options: Answering 'What do you want?' with a picture
Commenting on things the person sees
Naming pictures that staff point to
Starting a request by handing over a picture
A.why: PECS begins with physically assisted exchange and then distance and persistence: the person learns to approach a partner and initiate a request by handing over a picture.

whyNot.0: Responding to 'What do you want?' is phase 5.
whyNot.1: Commenting is phase 6, the final phase.
whyNot.2: Naming pictures on request is not the PECS focus; initiation is.

A.q: Which is an example of an object of reference?
options: A spoon given to a person just before each meal
A photo board showing the person's family
A symbol card for 'toilet' on the bathroom door
A tablet app that speaks a chosen word aloud
A.why: An object of reference is a real object that stands for an activity, person or place, such as a spoon meaning 'meal time'.

whyNot.1: Photos are pictorial, not objects of reference.
whyNot.2: A symbol card is a picture symbol, used by people who understand symbols.
whyNot.3: A speech-generating app is electronic AAC, not an object of reference.

B.q: Noor, 17, is autistic and uses PECS at phase 4. On the ward she hands the nurse a sentence strip with 'I want' and a picture of juice. What is the best response?
options: Ask her to say the word 'juice' before giving it
Point to the picture and sign 'juice' back to her
Give her the juice promptly and name it as you do
Explain that drinks are given at set times on the ward
B.why: In PECS the exchange is honoured promptly so the person learns that communication works. Naming the item models language.

whyNot.0: Demanding speech before responding undermines the exchange she has made.
whyNot.1: Signing back without giving the item does not honour her request.
whyNot.3: Delaying without explanation in her mode teaches that her request did not work.

B.q: A nurse plans to use Makaton with Tom, 45, who has a moderate learning disability and unclear speech. Which practice is most appropriate?
options: Sign the key words while speaking the full sentence
Sign every word of the sentence without speaking
Use written words with Tom in place of signs
Use signs during handover between staff members
B.why: Makaton is used with speech, signing key words in spoken word order to give extra clues.

whyNot.1: Makaton accompanies speech; signing without speech removes a channel.
whyNot.2: Written words may not be accessible to Tom; signs and symbols support speech.
whyNot.3: Signing between staff does not help Tom's communication.

B.q: Bethany, 29, has profound and multiple learning disabilities. Staff want her to anticipate daily activities. Why might objects of reference suit her better than photographs?
options: Photographs are not recommended for adults
Objects are easier to store in her bedroom
Objects can be understood through touch and use
Photographs need speech therapy approval to use
B.why: Objects of reference suit people who find pictures and signs hard; they can be felt, held and linked directly to the activity.

whyNot.0: Photos are used with adults who understand them.
whyNot.1: Storage is not the reason; meaning through touch and use is.
whyNot.3: Photographs do not need approval; the issue is whether Bethany understands them.

C.q: Callum, 21, has a severe learning disability and visual impairment. At home a towel means bath time. On the ward, a nurse uses a flannel instead because the towel is in the laundry. Callum becomes distressed. What is the best explanation and action?
options: He dislikes washing; offer a later bath time
He is in pain; give the prescribed analgesia
He is tired; postpone washing until tomorrow
The object changed; use his own towel each time
C.why: An object of reference works through consistency. A different object does not carry the same meaning, so Callum cannot anticipate what is happening.

whyNot.0: Nothing suggests he dislikes washing; the change in object is the obvious trigger.
whyNot.1: Pain should be considered if distress continues, but the change in object explains the timing.
whyNot.2: Postponing does not fix the communication problem for the next wash.

C.q: Jai, 8, is autistic and is learning PECS. A nurse holds up three pictures and asks him to point to the one he wants. His parents say this is not how PECS works for him. Which reason is most accurate?
options: PECS uses written words rather than pictures
PECS is based on Jai starting the exchange himself
PECS is used by speech therapists and not by nurses
PECS uses signs with speech in spoken word order
C.why: PECS teaches the person to initiate by handing over a picture. Holding up choices and asking him to point is a different approach.

whyNot.0: PECS uses pictures, building to sentence strips.
whyNot.2: Anyone supporting Jai can respond to PECS exchanges once they know how.

C.q: A ward is admitting four people with a learning disability. Which person's communication plan most clearly indicates the use of Makaton?
options: Ana: no speech, understands some spoken words and copies gestures
Bilal: visual impairment, responds to familiar objects by touch
Cara: autistic, uses a picture book to make requests
Dev: fluent reader, prefers written step-by-step lists
C.why: Makaton signs help people with no speech or unclear speech; Ana understands some words and imitates gestures, so signs with speech fit her.

whyNot.1: Object-based, touch communication points to objects of reference.
whyNot.2: A picture book for requests points to PECS.
whyNot.3: A fluent reader is likely to be served by written information.

reteach.title: Words you can see or hold
reteach.question: If spoken words do not work for someone, what can carry the meaning instead?

blocks.body: Makaton turns key words into signs and symbols you can see, alongside speech. PECS turns requests into pictures the person hands to you. Objects of reference turn activities into things the person can hold. The meaning stays the same; the form changes to one the person can use.

blocks.text: Consistency is the rule for all three: the same sign, the same picture, the same object, every time, by every member of staff.

explain.body: Symbols, signs and speech together. Signs are used with speech in spoken word order. Core Vocabulary first, then a larger Resource Vocabulary.

test.q: Which vocabulary in Makaton is taught first?
options: The Resource Vocabulary
The Topic Vocabulary
The Core Vocabulary
The Symbol Vocabulary
test.why: The Core Vocabulary of essential words is taught first and is the foundation; the larger Resource Vocabulary is used as needed.

whyNot.0: The Resource Vocabulary is the larger, topic-based bank used later.
whyNot.1: Topic-based signs sit in the Resource Vocabulary.
whyNot.3: Symbols match concepts across both vocabularies; there is no separate symbol vocabulary taught first.

explain.body: 1 physically assisted exchange, 2 distance and persistence, 3 picture discrimination, 4 sentence structure, 5 responding to 'What do you want?', 6 commenting.

test.q: A child using PECS has started choosing between two pictures. Which phase is this?
options: Phase 1: physically assisted exchange
Phase 4: sentence structure
Phase 6: commenting
Phase 3: picture discrimination
test.why: Choosing between pictures is phase 3, picture discrimination.

whyNot.0: Phase 1 is a single assisted exchange without choice.

explain.body: A real object stands for an activity, person or place. It helps the person anticipate, understand when something is finished and make choices.

test.q: Who is most likely to benefit from objects of reference?
options: A person who reads easy read leaflets
A person who does not yet use pictures
A person who uses sentence strips
A person who signs in full sentences
test.why: Objects of reference suit people who find speech, signs, photos and symbols hard to use or understand.

whyNot.0: Reading easy read shows the person uses pictures and text.
whyNot.2: Sentence strips are PECS phase 4, so the person uses pictures.
whyNot.3: Full signing shows an established sign system.

explain.body: Bring in the person's own book, cards or objects. Use them the same way every time, respond promptly and record them so every shift does the same.

test.q: A woman's PECS book is left at home on admission. What should the nurse do?
options: Make a new book from ward pictures
Ask her family to bring her book in
Use speech until she goes home
Wait for the SLT to visit the ward
test.why: Her own book has the pictures she knows. Getting it brought in restores her communication quickly.

whyNot.0: New unfamiliar pictures may not carry meaning for her.
whyNot.2: Relying on speech removes her main means of requesting.
whyNot.3: Waiting delays her ability to communicate.
